claim: The eukaryotic RNA exosome is a conserved and essential multisubunit complex that carries out diverse functions in RNA metabolism, ranging from normal turnover, processing and maturation, to quality control.
source: The eukaryotic RNA exosome is a conserved and essential multisubunit complex that carries out diverse functions in RNA metabolism, ranging from normal turnover, processing and maturation, to quality control (Kilchert et al., 2016; Zinder and Lima, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kilchert et al., 2016; Zinder and Lima, 2017).

claim: In yeast, the 9-subunit exosome core (Exo9) forms a donut-shaped scaffold that recruits two 3' to 5' exoribonucleases, Dis3 (aka Rrp44) and Rrp6.
source: In yeast, its 9-subunit core (Exo9) forms a donut-shaped scaffold that recruits two 3' to 5' exoribonucleases, Dis3 (aka Rrp44) and Rrp6.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about yeast exosome structure and composition.

claim: Exo9 and Dis3 form the cytoplasmic exosome (Exo10Dis3).
source: Subunit composition of RNA exosomes varies according to cellular localization, where Exo9 and Dis3 form the cytoplasmic exosome (Exo10Dis3), and Exo9, Dis3, and Rrp6 constitute the nuclear exosome (Exo11Dis3/Rrp6).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about exosome localization and composition.

claim: Exo9, Dis3, and Rrp6 constitute the nuclear exosome (Exo11Dis3/Rrp6).
source: Subunit composition of RNA exosomes varies according to cellular localization, where Exo9 and Dis3 form the cytoplasmic exosome (Exo10Dis3), and Exo9, Dis3, and Rrp6 constitute the nuclear exosome (Exo11Dis3/Rrp6).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about exosome localization and composition.

claim: Human Exo9 and Rrp6 may form a nucleolar exosome (Exo10Rrp6).
source: Additionally, human Exo9 and Rrp6 may form a nucleolar exosome (Exo10Rrp6) (Tomecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tomecki et al., 2010.

claim: Nuclear RNA exosome activities are associated with an astounding repertoire of RNA substrates, including precursors of ribosomal RNA, snoRNAs, snRNAs, surveillance of tRNA and pre-mRNAs, and decay of non-coding RNAs including CUTs, PROMPTs, and eRNAs.
source: Nuclear RNA exosome activities are associated with an astounding repertoire of RNA substrates, including precursors of ribosomal RNA, snoRNAs, snRNAs, surveillance of tRNA and pre-mRNAs, and decay of non-coding RNAs including CUTs, PROMPTs, and eRNAs (Allmang et al., 1999, 2000; Basu et al., 2011; Houseley et al., 2006; Pefanis et al., 2015; Schneider et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutations in exosome subunits and its misregulation have been reported in several diseases.
source: Not surprisingly, mutations in exosome subunits and its misregulation have been reported in several diseases (Fasken et al., 2017; Lohr et al., 2014; Robinson et al., 2015; Wan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Exo9 modulates the activities of Dis3 and Rrp6.
source: Specifically, these studies revealed that Exo9 modulates the activities of Dis3 and Rrp6; that the Rrp6 protein can stimulate Dis3 (Liu et al., 2006; Wasmuth and Lima, 2012; Wasmuth et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Rrp6 protein can stimulate Dis3.
source: Specifically, these studies revealed that Exo9 modulates the activities of Dis3 and Rrp6; that the Rrp6 protein can stimulate Dis3 (Liu et al., 2006; Wasmuth and Lima, 2012; Wasmuth et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The major path for RNAs greater than 30 nucleotides utilize the Exo9 central channel to guide RNA to Rrp6 for distributive trimming or through the entire channel to Dis3 for processive decay.
source: that the major path for RNAs greater than 30 nucleotides utilize the Exo9 central channel to guide RNA to Rrp6 for distributive trimming or through the entire channel to Dis3 for processive decay (Bonneau et al., 2009; Drazkowska et al., 2013; Malet et al., 2010; Wasmuth and Lima, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There exists a minor channel-independent 'direct access' route to Dis3 for shorter RNAs.
source: and the existence of a minor channel-independent 'direct access' route to Dis3 for shorter RNAs (Liu et al., 2014; Makino et al., 2015; Zinder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual deletion of Mpp6 or Rrp47 in vivo results in misprocessing of nuclear exosome substrates.
source: The nuclear exosome is associated with the protein cofactors Mpp6 and Rrp47, whose individual deletion in vivo results in misprocessing of nuclear exosome substrates, while concomitant loss leads to synthetic lethality (Butler and Mitchell, 2011; Feigenbutz et al., 2013a; Milligan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Concomitant loss of Mpp6 and Rrp47 leads to synthetic lethality.
source: The nuclear exosome is associated with the protein cofactors Mpp6 and Rrp47, whose individual deletion in vivo results in misprocessing of nuclear exosome substrates, while concomitant loss leads to synthetic lethality (Butler and Mitchell, 2011; Feigenbutz et al., 2013a; Milligan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TRAMP complex catalyzes polyadenylation and subsequent degradation of an array of nuclear RNAs.
source: These genetic observations resemble deletions of the TRAMP complex, a three protein complex that catalyzes polyadenylation and subsequent degradation of an array of nuclear RNAs (LaCava et al., 2005; Vanácová et al., 2005; Wyers et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TRAMP complex consists of one of two non-templated polyA polymerases Trf4/5, one of two zinc knuckle proteins Air1/2, and the essential RNA helicase Mtr4.
source: through one of two non-templated polyA polymerases Trf4/5, one of two zinc knuckle proteins Air1/2, and the essential RNA helicase Mtr4, which is thought to bridge the nuclear exosome to other RNPs, including ribosome biogenesis factors (Thoms et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thoms et al., 2015.

claim: Mtr4 is thought to bridge the nuclear exosome to other RNPs, including ribosome biogenesis factors.
source: through one of two non-templated polyA polymerases Trf4/5, one of two zinc knuckle proteins Air1/2, and the essential RNA helicase Mtr4, which is thought to bridge the nuclear exosome to other RNPs, including ribosome biogenesis factors (Thoms et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thoms et al., 2015 and involves speculative reasoning about Mtr4 function.

claim: Rrp47 binds directly to Rrp6 via the Rrp6 N-terminal domain.
source: Indeed, Rrp47 binds directly to Rrp6 via the Rrp6 N-terminal domain, an interaction that stabilizes Rrp6 (Dedic et al., 2014; Feigenbutz et al., 2013a, 2013b; Stead et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interaction between Rrp47 and Rrp6 stabilizes Rrp6.
source: Indeed, Rrp47 binds directly to Rrp6 via the Rrp6 N-terminal domain, an interaction that stabilizes Rrp6 (Dedic et al., 2014; Feigenbutz et al., 2013a, 2013b; Stead et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rrp47 and Rrp6 generate a composite interface that recruits Mtr4.
source: and generates a composite interface that recruits Mtr4 (Schuch et al., 2014) in vitro and in vivo, though other factors are speculated to exist (Feigenbutz et al., 2013b; Schuch et al., 2014; Stuparevic et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schuch et al., 2014.

claim: Mpp6 function is less clear, due in part to its poor sequence conservation.
source: In contrast, Mpp6 function is less clear, due in part to its poor sequence conservation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the state of knowledge about Mpp6.

claim: Synthetic lethality of Mpp6 with Rrp6 in yeast suggested Mpp6 may be a Dis3 cofactor.
source: Its synthetic lethality with Rrp6 in yeast suggested Mpp6 may be a Dis3 cofactor (Milligan et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Milligan et al., 2008 and involves speculation about Mpp6 function.

claim: In human, Mpp6 was posited as a Rrp6 cofactor.
source: while in human it was posited as a Rrp6 cofactor (Schilders et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schilders et al., 2005.

claim: Mpp6 has been reported to recruit Mtr4.
source: and has been reported to recruit Mtr4 (Chen et al., 2001; Lim et al., 2017; Lubas et al., 2011; Schilders et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast Mpp6 bound flexible RNAs most tightly, with a Kd of 170 nM for polyU RNA, and a Kd of 62 nM for AU-rich RNA.
source: Similar to previous results (Milligan et al., 2008; Schilders et al., 2005), yeast Mpp6 bound flexible RNAs most tightly, with a Kd of 170 nM for polyU RNA, and a Kd of 62 nM for AU-rich RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mpp6 bound polyA RNA with a Kd of 1.4 µM.
source: Mpp6 also bound polyA RNA, albeit much weaker (Kd of 1.4 µM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mpp6 interacts with Exo9.
source: Consistent with previous results (Schuch et al., 2014), Mpp6 interacts with Exo9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analytical gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and a citation to Schuch et al., 2014.

claim: Mpp6 stimulated Rrp6-mediated decay 13-fold in the context of Exo10Rrp6.
source: In the context of Exo10Rrp6, Mpp6 stimulated Rrp6-mediated decay 13-fold (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mpp6 stimulated Rrp6 activity by 2.5-fold while reducing Dis3 activity by 1.5-fold when associated with Exo11Dis3/Rrp6.
source: Mpp6 stimulated Rrp6 activity by 2.5-fold while reducing Dis3 activity by 1.5-fold when associated with Exo11Dis3/Rrp6 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mpp6 had no effect on the activities of Rrp6 or Dis3 in isolation.
source: In contrast, Mpp6 had no effect on the activities of Rrp6 or Dis3 in isolation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Mpp6 failed to stimulate Dis3 exoribonuclease or endoribonuclease activity on polyA RNA when associated with Exo10Dis3.
source: and Mpp6 failed to stimulate Dis3 exoribonuclease or endoribonuclease activity on polyA RNA when associated with Exo10Dis3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mpp6 could stimulate Dis3 exoribonuclease activity by 3.5-fold in Exo11Dis3/Rrp6exo- when a catalytically inert mutant of Rrp6 (Rrp6exo-) was present.
source: However, Mpp6 could stimulate Dis3 exoribonuclease activity by 3.5-fold in Exo11Dis3/Rrp6exo- when a catalytically inert mutant of Rrp6 (Rrp6exo-) was present (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mpp6 had no detectable effect on Dis3 endoribonuclease activity.
source: Mpp6 had no detectable effect on Dis3 endoribonuclease activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mpp6 stimulated Exo10Rrp6 activity by only 1.6-fold using AU-rich RNA.
source: Although Mpp6 alone bound AU-rich RNA over 20 times better than polyA RNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), Mpp6 stimulated Exo10Rrp6 activity by only 1.6-fold using this RNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Mpp6 exerted a 4-fold increase in Exo10Dis3 exoribonuclease activity for AU-rich RNA.
source: In contrast, Mpp6 exerted a greater effect on Exo10Dis3 for AU-rich RNA, with a 4-fold increase in exoribonuclease activity and 9.5-fold tighter binding for AU-rich RNA (14 nM versus 130 nM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Mpp6 exerted a 9.5-fold tighter binding for AU-rich RNA (14 nM versus 130 nM) in Exo10Dis3.
source: In contrast, Mpp6 exerted a greater effect on Exo10Dis3 for AU-rich RNA, with a 4-fold increase in exoribonuclease activity and 9.5-fold tighter binding for AU-rich RNA (14 nM versus 130 nM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Activation of Rrp6 in Exo11Dis3/Rrp6 only required a central region within Mpp6 that included residues 81–120.
source: Activation of Rrp6 in Exo11Dis3/Rrp6 only required a central region within Mpp6 that included residues 81–120 (Figure 1C), hereafter referred to as 'Mpp6Minimal', as other regions were dispensable for activation of Rrp6 in exosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays with Mpp6 truncations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/Channel-occ bound polyA RNA with a Kd of 210 nM.
source: Binding measurements could not be reliably determined for Exo10Rrp6exo-/Channel-occ (>10 µM); however, Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/Channel-occ bound polyA RNA with a Kd of 210 nM, 3.8 fold tighter than Exo10Rrp6exo-/WTchannel+ (780 nM), but 2.3 times weaker than Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/WTchannel+ (92 nM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Exo10Rrp6exo-/WTchannel+ bound polyA RNA with a Kd of 780 nM.
source: Binding measurements could not be reliably determined for Exo10Rrp6exo-/Channel-occ (>10 µM); however, Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/Channel-occ bound polyA RNA with a Kd of 210 nM, 3.8 fold tighter than Exo10Rrp6exo-/WTchannel+ (780 nM), but 2.3 times weaker than Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/WTchannel+ (92 nM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/WTchannel+ bound polyA RNA with a Kd of 92 nM.
source: Binding measurements could not be reliably determined for Exo10Rrp6exo-/Channel-occ (>10 µM); however, Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/Channel-occ bound polyA RNA with a Kd of 210 nM, 3.8 fold tighter than Exo10Rrp6exo-/WTchannel+ (780 nM), but 2.3 times weaker than Exo10Rrp6exo-/Mpp6/WTchannel+ (92 nM) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Mpp6 cooperates with elements within the exosome to bind RNA more tightly in a manner that is partially dependent on the integrity of the Exo9 central channel.
source: As Mpp6 on its own binds polyA RNA with a Kd of 1.4 µM (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), it appears that Mpp6 cooperates with elements within the exosome to bind RNA more tightly in a manner that is partially dependent on the integrity of the Exo9 central channel.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing Mpp6 binding alone versus in complex with exosome variants.

claim: Mpp6 partially rescued defects of S1/KH ring mutations, but the complexes were less active when compared to wild-type Exo10Rrp6.
source: Although Mpp6 partially rescued defects of these S1/KH ring mutations, the complexes were less active when compared to wild-type Exo10Rrp6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), suggesting that Mpp6-bound exosomes use a similar RNA path to that observed previously to guide RNA to Rrp6 (Wasmuth et al., 2014; Wasmuth and Lima, 2012; Zinder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Mpp6-bound exosomes use a similar RNA path to that observed previously to guide RNA to Rrp6.
source: Although Mpp6 partially rescued defects of these S1/KH ring mutations, the complexes were less active when compared to wild-type Exo10Rrp6 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), suggesting that Mpp6-bound exosomes use a similar RNA path to that observed previously to guide RNA to Rrp6 (Wasmuth et al., 2014; Wasmuth and Lima, 2012; Zinder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The crystal structure of Exo12Dis3exo-endo-/Rrp6exo-/Mpp6Min was determined to a resolution of 3.3 Å.
source: The crystal structure of Exo12Dis3exo-endo-/Rrp6exo-/Mpp6Min was determined to a resolution of 3.3 Å (Table 1, Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1 and Figure 2A.

claim: One RNA 3' end is anchored in the Dis3 active site with Dis3 adopting a 'direct access' conformation.
source: Analogous to the previous structure, one RNA 3' end is anchored in the Dis3 active site with Dis3 adopting a 'direct access' conformation (Han and van Hoof, 2016; Liu et al., 2014; Makino et al., 2015; Zinder et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The other RNA 3' end is anchored in the Rrp6 active site of an adjacent complex.
source: while the other 3' end is anchored in the Rrp6 active site of an adjacent complex (Zinder et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and a citation to Zinder et al., 2016.

claim: Electron densities for Mpp6 residues 90 to 118 were evident on the surface of Rrp40.
source: Electron densities for Mpp6 residues 90 to 118 were evident on the surface of Rrp40 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mpp6Minimal residues 90–97 adopt a distorted parallel beta-strand configuration that complements the second beta-strand of the Rrp40 N-terminal domain (NTD).
source: Mpp6Minimal residues 90–97 adopt a distorted parallel beta-strand configuration that complements the second beta-strand of the Rrp40 N-terminal domain (NTD) while residues 98–103 adopt a helical conformation that wedges between the Rrp40 NTD and S1 domain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mpp6 residues 98–103 adopt a helical conformation that wedges between the Rrp40 NTD and S1 domain.
source: Mpp6Minimal residues 90–97 adopt a distorted parallel beta-strand configuration that complements the second beta-strand of the Rrp40 N-terminal domain (NTD) while residues 98–103 adopt a helical conformation that wedges between the Rrp40 NTD and S1 domain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mpp6 residues 110–118 adopt an anti-parallel beta-strand conformation that complements the second beta-strand of the KH domain.
source: Mpp6 residues 110–118 adopt an anti-parallel beta-strand conformation that complements the second beta-strand of the KH domain (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Contacts observed in the structure are consistent with crosslinking and mass spectrometry data reported previously, including crosslinks between Rrp40 Lys176 and Mpp6 Lys113 and between Rrp40 Lys49 and Mpp6 Lys104.
source: Contacts observed in our structure are also consistent with crosslinking and mass spectrometry data reported previously, including crosslinks between Rrp40 Lys176 and Mpp6 Lys113 and between Rrp40 Lys49 and Mpp6 Lys104 (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data and a citation to Shi et al., 2015.

claim: Exosomes lacking Rrp40 could not associate with Mpp6.

claim: Mpp6 did not stimulate Rrp6 activity in exosomes lacking Rrp40.
source: Consistent with the structural data, exosomes lacking Rrp40 could not associate with Mpp6, and Mpp6 did not stimulate Rrp6 activity in exosomes lacking Rrp40 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA degradation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Interactions could not be detected between Rrp40 and Mpp6 in isolation.
source: Although Mpp6 interacts directly with Rrp40 in the context of the exosome complex, interactions could not be detected between Rrp40 and Mpp6 in isolation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analytical gel filtration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mpp6 residues 81 to 90, which are disordered in the structure, are required for exosome Rrp6 stimulation.
source: Furthermore, Mpp6 residues 81 to 90, which are disordered in our structure, are required for exosome Rrp6 stimulation (Figure 1C).

claim: Mpp6 residues Leu92, Ile93 and Ile94 reside in the first beta strand and are nestled into a hydrophobic surface of the Rrp40 NTD.
source: Mpp6 residues Leu92, Ile93 and Ile94 reside in the first beta strand and are nestled into a hydrophobic surface of the Rrp40 NTD (Figure 3B).

claim: The hydrophobic quality of Mpp6 residues Leu92, Ile93 and Ile94 is conserved within eukaryotes, despite divergent sequence.
source: The hydrophobic quality of these Mpp6 residues is conserved within eukaryotes, despite divergent sequence (Figure 3A).

claim: Mpp6 Tyr99 and Leu102 pack into a hydrophobic pocket created by Rrp40 Pro23 and Tyr56.

claim: Mpp6 Tyr99 is conserved as tyrosine, phenylalanine or leucine in other Mpp6 family members.
source: While Mpp6 residues 101–103 are not conserved across evolution, Tyr99 is conserved as tyrosine, phenylalanine or leucine in other Mpp6 family members.

claim: Mpp6 Phe115 contacts Rrp40 Phe184.
source: Additional hydrophobic interactions are observed within the last beta strand of Mpp6, including contacts between Mpp6 Phe115 and Rrp40 Phe184 (Figure 3B).

claim: In yeast through man, the corresponding residue to Mpp6 Phe115 is either a phenylalanine or tryptophan.

claim: Mpp6 Arg112 projects into a pocket formed between the S1 and KH domains of Rrp40.

claim: Mpp6 Arg112 is within hydrogen bond distance to the Glu185 side chain carboxylate and the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Gly146.

claim: Rrp40 Glu185 and Gly146 are strictly conserved in Rrp40.
source: Arg112 is within hydrogen bond distance to the Glu185 side chain carboxylate and the backbone carbonyl oxygen of Gly146 (Figure 3B), residues that are not known to be involved in other interactions and are strictly conserved in Rrp40.

claim: Rrp40 Gly148 (Gly191 in human) is mutated to cysteine in hereditary spastic paraplegia in humans.

claim: Rrp40 Trp195 (Trp238 in human) is mutated to arginine in pontocerebeller hypoplasia and spinal motor neuron degeneration.
source: and Trp195 (Trp238 in human), which is mutated to arginine in pontocerebeller hypoplasia and spinal motor neuron degeneration (Wan et al., 2012).

claim: Three of the four Mpp6 arginine mutants (R89E, R103E, R112E) were defective in stimulating Exo10Rrp6 activity using polyA RNA.

claim: Mpp6 R112E exhibited the greatest defect in stimulating Exo10Rrp6 activity.

claim: The defect on Exo10Rrp6 stimulation observed for Mpp6 R89E was exacerbated when combined with Rrp40 E185A.

claim: The defect in exosome stimulation by Mpp6 R103E could be overcome by adding 10-fold excess mutant Mpp6.

claim: Combining Mpp6 R112E and Rrp40 E185A resulted in a similar loss of stimulation.

claim: Mpp6 association is required for stimulation of Rrp6 in the nuclear RNA exosome.
source: These results are consistent with contacts observed in the structure and suggest that Mpp6 association is required for stimulation of Rrp6 in the nuclear RNA exosome.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data on Mpp6 mutants.

claim: The first modeled residue of Mpp6Minimal (Pro90) is located 13 Å away from the last modeled amino acids of the Rrp6 CTD (Phe618) and Rrp43 NTD (Thr9).
source: The first modeled residue of Mpp6Minimal (Pro90) is located 13 Å away from the last modeled amino acids of the Rrp6 CTD (Phe618) and Rrp43 NTD (Thr9) as observed in previous structures of Rrp6-associated exosomes (Figure 4A) (Makino et al., 2013, 2015; Wasmuth et al., 2014; Zinder et al., 2016).

claim: The Rrp6 lasso includes the last one hundred residues and was recently reported to stimulate the activities of the nuclear exosome.

claim: The Rrp6 lasso is important for stimulation by Mpp6.

claim: The Rrp6 CTD activated Exo10Dis3 by 3-fold.
